transcript:
Header: 2027-08-31 15:00 PDT | Duration: 45m | Attendees: Maya Shah, Carlos Mendes (Redwood); Priya Rao, Ben Carter, Aisha Khan, Leo Park (Skyline)

Auto-summary (optional): Focus on reducing Time-To-First-Token and improving streaming behavior for 7B variant; profiling plan agreed.

00:00 Speaker 1 (Maya): Hey everyone, thanks for joining. Quick check, audio ok?
00:07 Speaker 2 (Priya): Yep, good here, thanks.
00:10 Speaker 1 (Maya): Great. Recap from last week — we saw some TTFT spikes around 380-420ms on the 7B run when sequence length got to 900 plus, and streaming wasn't delivering early chunks fast enough. Carlos, want to take us through the profiling you ran?
00:29 Speaker 3 (Carlos): Sure, yeah so I ran two passes, one with streaming enabled and small chunk size and one fully buffered. The TTFT for cold cache was around 170ms on the 1.3B, avg token latencies were good, but on 7B we saw kernel launch overhead plus fragmentation in the KV cache, uh, the transcriber wrote K V cash earlier but it's KV cache.
00:54 Speaker 4 (Ben): Sorry, can you repeat the numbers for the 7B? I got muted for a sec.
00:58 Speaker 3 (Carlos): Yeah, so cold TTFT 7B was about 380ms when sequence length was ~1k and batch size small; warm cache (prefix cached) dropped to ~110-130ms. Streaming first-byte with small chunking hit around 240ms because of serialization overhead.
01:20 Speaker 2 (Priya): Hmm, that matches what we saw in logs. We care a lot about first byte because product wants sub-300ms perceived latency for single-turn flows.
01:31 Speaker 1 (Maya): Right, and there's the tradeoff: smaller chunk sends improve perceived TTFT but increase compute overhead and network packets; larger chunking lowers tokens/sec efficiency.
01:42 Speaker 5 (Aisha): Do we have a recommended chunk size? We tried 64 token chunks and it felt jittery.
01:50 Speaker 3 (Carlos): For our runtime we've found 128 tokens is a decent balance for 7B on A100-ish hardware; 64 can work but you pay for kernel overhead. Also quantization profile matters — int8/4x4 choices change kernel selection and memory layout which affects kernel launch times.
02:14 Speaker 4 (Ben): On our side we're on v5 nVidia fleet with mixed GPUs, not all identical — any implications there?
02:22 Speaker 3 (Carlos): Yes, heterogeneous GPUs will make kernel selection harder; runtime picks per-device kernels but worst-case you get slowest device bottleneck. For the pilot we recommend pinning the 7B variant to a homogeneous pool or using model variant routing.
02:38 Speaker 6 (Leo): We can carve a homogeneous pool for pilot — will need to check capacity.
02:43 Speaker 1 (Maya): Thanks Leo. Quick note on sequence length distribution — Priya, you mentioned in Slack you have long few-shot prompts occasionally?
02:51 Speaker 2 (Priya): Yeah about 5% of our calls hit >1k because of multi-turn context, examples, and legal boilerplate. Most are <350 tokens.
03:02 Speaker 3 (Carlos): That distribution explains the tail we'll see. Padding to max length is expensive, so we suggested bucketing by length and using dynamic batching. Also prefix KV caching for repeated system prompts helps a lot.
03:20 Speaker 2 (Priya): About KV cache, we noticed some cache thrashing when requests varied; is there a recommended TTL or policy?
03:27 Speaker 3 (Carlos): TTL is workload dependent; for high reuse keep it longer, but memory pressure can evict. We can tune cache sizing and pin the common system prompt to the GPU RAM to avoid recompute.
03:38 Speaker 5 (Aisha): On streaming, any quick wins to reduce TTFT without sacrificing throughput?
03:44 Speaker 3 (Carlos): Two quick wins: 1) send an initial header token earlier (early send heuristic) so the client gets something immediately, 2) smaller warm-up prompt engine — move heavy preprocessing off the critical path. But measure — early send can look like lower TTFT but may raise overall tokens/sec cost.
04:04 Speaker 4 (Ben): Does Redwood runtime support chunked streaming with partial tokenization? We need to integrate with our front-end.
04:11 Speaker 3 (Carlos): Yes, we support streaming at token boundary level and also partial chunks; we'll share the API snippet. There's also function calling/structured output but that's separate.
04:24 Speaker 1 (Maya): We're going to push a new benchmark artifact — spreadsheet with TTFT vs chunk size, vs sequence length and vs kernel choices. We'll also add a column for perceived latency (first-byte).
04:37 Speaker 2 (Priya): That'll be helpful. Also can you annotate rows with which runs were warm vs cold cache?
04:43 Speaker 3 (Carlos): Yes will do.
04:45 Speaker 1 (Maya): Ok quick security note — Priya asked about private deployment earlier. For this pilot we can do Redwood Dedicated with VPC peering; we have SOC2 certs and KMS options. We'll email the security doc link.
04:58 Speaker 2 (Priya): Please include audit log examples and retention options — legal will pick at audit.
05:05 Speaker 1 (Maya): Will do.
05:07 Speaker 3 (Carlos): Back to kernel choices — for 1.3B int8 is fine and gives good latency; for 7B int4/4x4 can help memory but sometimes forces slower kernels on certain GPUs. We'll profile both.
05:23 Speaker 6 (Leo): Any network considerations? We saw occasional TCP spikes during concurrent requests.
05:29 Speaker 3 (Carlos): Keep the control plane separated and peer over private link; also tune kernel batch size and use connection pooling. We can provide recommended TCP tuning knobs.
05:42 Speaker 5 (Aisha): For acceptance criteria — Priya, what do you need to see in the pilot to be comfortable?
05:48 Speaker 2 (Priya): We need TTFT <300ms 95th for single-turn flows, streaming first-byte <250ms perceived, and overall cost under X (we agreed to share target later). Also audit and SSO must be ok.
06:05 Speaker 1 (Maya): Good. We'll align next week on profiling results. Carlos, timeline for the kernel runs?
06:11 Speaker 3 (Carlos): I can run them tomorrow and post results by Friday, given access to the prompt set. If you can drop the sample prompts by Monday we'll be fine.
06:22 Speaker 2 (Priya): I'll get the prompts to you Monday.
06:25 Speaker 1 (Maya): Great. Quick recap of next steps: Redwood sends updated benchmark spreadsheet and security docs, Carlos runs kernel profiling, Skyline shares prompts and infra details, schedule streaming deep dive next week.
06:42 Speaker 4 (Ben): Sounds good.
06:45 Speaker 1 (Maya): Thanks everyone, we'll send notes and action items in email. Bye.
06:50 Speaker 2 (Priya): Bye, thanks.

References/shared artifacts noted: benchmark_spreadsheet.xlsx (link shared in chat), security_compliance_packet.pdf (SOC2/KMS examples), kernel_profiling_script.sh (SE internal).

End of transcript.
